The 1968 Summer Olympics. The 1968 Summer Olympics in Mexico City became a watershed moment when African American sprinters Tommie Smith and John Carlos transformed the Games into a platform for civil rights protest and forced the world to reckon with politics in sport.

The city's high altitude, at two thousand two hundred fifty meters above sea level, enhanced performance in sprint events but challenged endurance athletes. Tommie Smith won gold in the two hundred meter dash, and John Carlos won bronze in the same event. During the medal ceremony, both athletes raised their black-gloved fists and bowed their heads during the national anthem in a gesture of solidarity with the Black Power movement.

The salute provoked international controversy. The International Olympic Committee suspended both athletes and banned them from the Olympic village, framing their protest as unsportsmanlike. The IOC's response exposed deep tensions around whether the Games could or should remain politically neutral.

Others protested as well. Wyomia Tyus, an African American woman who won gold in the one hundred meter dash, also protested by turning her back during the anthem. But she received far less media attention than Smith and Carlos, a disparity that reflected broader patterns in sports coverage.

The Games highlighted the Olympic principle of political neutrality, which activists directly challenged as complicit with racism and inequality. At the same time, Mexican student protests demanding democratic reforms had occurred before the Games; the government's violent response in the Tlatelolco massacre was largely overshadowed in international coverage by the Games themselves. The 1968 Olympics mark a turning point where the Games became understood as inevitably political—a platform where athletes could no longer remain silent on injustice.
